questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The wave function $\psi$, representing the state of four different electrons are shown below. Which electron has the smallest uncertainty in its momentum? [Graphs of $\psi$ against $x$: A a continuous sinusoid of constant amplitude across the whole range; B a wave packet of moderate width with several oscillations, largest in the centre; C a single smooth hump (Gaussian-like) in the middle; D a narrow wave packet with short-wavelength oscillations.] A B C D

stemImage.alt: Question 28: The wave function , representing the state of four different electrons are shown below. Which electron has the smallest uncertainty in its momentum?

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must link spatial extent of the wavefunction to $\Delta x$ and then use the uncertainty principle.
questions.misconception: Thinking a localised wave packet has a well-defined momentum

explanation.body: The key compares how spread out the probability density $|\psi|^2$ is. In A, equally high peaks recur across the graph, while B, C and D are concentrated near the centre. Using the position–momentum uncertainty principle, the key takes A’s greater spread in position to indicate the smallest spread in momentum.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the key’s choice based on the broad spatial spread.
perOption.B: Its probability density is concentrated more strongly near the centre than A’s.
perOption.C: Its probability density is concentrated near the centre, so the key rejects it on the basis of spatial extent.
perOption.D: Its probability density is concentrated near the centre within a narrow envelope.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The spectrum of a giant, glowing cloud of gas and dust in space, known as a nebula, is shown below together with the emission line spectra of four elements.

Which elements are present in the nebula?
questions.stemText: The spectrum of a giant, glowing cloud of gas and dust in space, known as a nebula, is shown below together with the emission line spectra of four elements. Which elements are present in the nebula? A helium and hydrogen B helium, hydrogen and krypton C helium, hydrogen, nitrogen and krypton D nitrogen and krypton

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Pattern matching of line spectra; must check that all lines of an element appear.
questions.misconception: Concluding an element is present when only some of its lines match

explanation.body: Compare the positions of each element’s emission lines with the lines in the nebula spectrum. All the lines shown for helium and hydrogen match. Nitrogen and krypton each have lines missing from the nebula spectrum.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Includes krypton even though some of its lines are missing.
perOption.C: Includes nitrogen and krypton even though neither has a complete match.
perOption.D: Omits helium and hydrogen, whose lines match, and includes two incomplete matches.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: An electron can have both wave and particle properties. Which equation relates the wavelength of an electron to one of its particle properties? A wavelength $\times$ momentum = constant B $\frac{\text{wavelength}}{\text{momentum}}$ = constant C wavelength $\times$ kinetic energy = constant D $\frac{\text{wavelength}}{\text{kinetic energy}}$ = constant

stemImage.alt: Question 27: An electron can have both wave and particle properties. Which equation relates the wavelength of an electron to one of its particle properties?

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the de Broglie relation $\lambda = h/p$.
questions.misconception: Confusing which particle property the de Broglie wavelength depends on, or inverting the relationship

explanation.body: The de Broglie equation is $\lambda=h/p$. Therefore $\lambda p=h$, where $h$ is Planck's constant.

perOption.A: Correct. The product is Planck's constant.
perOption.B: Makes wavelength directly proportional to momentum.
perOption.C: Substitutes kinetic energy for momentum, although the two are not proportional.
perOption.D: Makes wavelength increase with kinetic energy, although it decreases as momentum increases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The graphs show the variation with distance x of the square of the amplitude $|\psi |^{2}$ of the wavefunction of a particle.

Which graph corresponds to a particle with the largest uncertainty in momentum?
questions.stemText: The graphs show the variation with distance x of the square of the amplitude |ψ|2 of the wavefunction of a particle. Which graph corresponds to a particle with the largest uncertainty in momentum? A $|\psi |^{2}$ x / arbitrary units B $|\psi |^{2}$ x / arbitrary units C $|\psi |^{2}$ x / arbitrary units D $|\psi |^{2}$ x / arbitrary units

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Links the spread of $|\psi|^2$ to $\Delta x$ and applies the uncertainty principle qualitatively.
questions.misconception: Thinking a sharply peaked (well-localised) wavefunction means well-defined momentum

explanation.body: The graph of $\lvert\psi\rvert^2$ shows the position probability density. D has the narrowest peak, centred near $x=1.5$, and hence the smallest position uncertainty $\Delta x$. This gives the largest lower bound on $\Delta p$, which is the key's basis for choosing D.

perOption.A: The flat density spreads the particle across the region shown, giving weak localisation.
perOption.B: The probability is distributed across many peaks, giving a large position uncertainty.
perOption.C: The broad packet from about $x=0.0$ to $3.2$ gives a larger position uncertainty than D.
perOption.D: Correct. D is the most tightly localised in position.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two beams of monochromatic light have the same frequency. One beam has a greater intensity than the other beam.

How can the greater intensity of one beam be explained in terms of the particulate nature of light?
questions.stemText: Two beams of monochromatic light have the same frequency. One beam has a greater intensity than the other beam. How can the greater intensity of one beam be explained in terms of the particulate nature of light? A Each photon in the beam has more energy. B Each photon in the beam has greater speed. C The amplitude of oscillation is greater. D There are more photons passing through unit cross-sectional area of the beam per unit time.

options.label: A
options.text: Each photon in the beam has more energy.

options.label: B
options.text: Each photon in the beam has greater speed.

options.label: C
options.text: The amplitude of oscillation is greater.

options.label: D
options.text: There are more photons passing through unit cross-sectional area of the beam per unit time.

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard photon-flux explanation of intensity.
questions.misconception: Linking intensity to photon energy or wave amplitude

explanation.body: Intensity equals the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time multiplied by the energy per photon. The beams have the same frequency, so their photons carry the same energy. The more intense beam therefore has more photons crossing unit area each second.

perOption.A: Equal frequencies give equal photon energies.
perOption.B: All photons travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
perOption.C: Amplitude describes the electric and magnetic field oscillations in the wave picture.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: For an electron passing through a single slit, the uncertainty in its position $\Delta y$ and the uncertainty in its momentum $\Delta p$ are related by $\Delta y\,\Delta p \gtrsim h$. Which diagram shows the positions where $\Delta y$ and $\Delta p$ in the equation above are defined and shows them in the correct direction? [Each option shows a slit on the left and a screen on the right.] A $\Delta y$ vertical at the slit, $\Delta p$ vertical at the slit B $\Delta y$ vertical at the screen, $\Delta p$ vertical at the screen C $\Delta y$ vertical at the slit, $\Delta p$ horizontal (along travel) at the slit D $\Delta y$ vertical at the screen, $\Delta p$ horizontal at the slit

stemImage.alt: Question 28: For an electron passing through a single slit, the uncertainty in its position ∆y and the uncertainty in its momentum ∆p are related by Δy Δp ≳ h. Which diagram

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires understanding which position and momentum components the slit constrains.
questions.misconception: Taking $\Delta p$ along the direction of travel or $\Delta y$ at the screen

explanation.body: The slit confines the electron in the transverse $y$ direction, so $\Delta y$ is defined at the slit. The electrons spread in $y$ as they pass through, giving a transverse momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$. The uncertainty principle pairs position and momentum along the same axis.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Places both uncertainties at the screen, although the slit sets the position uncertainty used here.
perOption.C: Pairs a transverse position uncertainty with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.
perOption.D: Uses the screen for the position uncertainty and pairs it with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Which graph shows the relationship between photon energy $E$ and wavelength $\lambda$ of electromagnetic waves? [Graphs: A $E$ against $1/\lambda$, concave curve through origin levelling off; B $E$ against $1/\lambda$, straight line through origin; C $E$ against $\lambda$, straight line through origin; D $E$ against $\lambda$, concave curve through origin levelling off.]

stemImage.alt: Question 27: Which graph shows the relationship between photon energy E and wavelength λ of electromagnetic waves?

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall $E = hc/\lambda$ and recognise the linear graph against $1/\lambda$.
questions.misconception: Thinking photon energy increases with wavelength

explanation.body: Photon energy is $E=hf=hc/\lambda$, so $E$ is directly proportional to $1/\lambda$. The graph of $E$ against $1/\lambda$ is therefore a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Shows a nonlinear dependence on reciprocal wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes energy directly proportional to wavelength.
perOption.D: Shows energy increasing with wavelength even though it decreases.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A particle of mass m in a well of width L has ground-state energy E. A second particle has mass 2m and is confined in a well of width 2L. Its ground-state energy is:
questions.stemText: A particle of mass m in a well of width L has ground-state energy E. A second particle has mass 2m and is confined in a well of width 2L. Its ground-state energy is: A E 2 B E 4 C E 8 D E 16

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Ratio reasoning with $E \propto 1/(mL^2)$.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square the well width

explanation.body: The energy levels are $E_n=h^2n^2/(8mL^2)$, and the ground state has $n=1$, giving $E=h^2/(8mL^2)$. For the second particle, $E'=h^2/[8(2m)(2L)^2]=E/8$.

perOption.A: Accounts only for the doubling of mass.
perOption.B: Accounts only for the width doubling, or treats both effects as linear.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Squares the mass ratio as well as the width ratio.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A beam of electrons traveling at a constant speed in the x-direction passes through a horizontal single narrow slit of width $\Delta y$, in the vertical direction. According to Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle, what is the expected result as the slit is made increasingly narrower? A The uncertainty in the y-component of the electrons' momentum decreases, causing the beam to become highly focused in a straight line. B The uncertainty in the x-component of the electrons' momentum increases, causing the electrons to accelerate unpredictably after the slit. C The uncertainty in the y-component of the electrons' momentum increases, causing the electron beam to spread out more in the vertical direction after passing through the slit. D The momentum of the electrons remains unaffected because the uncertainty principle only applies to the emission of photons, not moving mass.

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A beam of electrons traveling at a constant speed in the x-direction passes through a horizontal single narrow slit of width y  , in the vertical direction. Ac

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Qualitative use of $\Delta y\,\Delta p_y \gtrsim h$ in a standard single-slit context.
questions.misconception: Thinking a narrower slit gives a more focused beam

explanation.body: The slit confines each electron’s vertical position to approximately the slit width $\Delta y$. Narrowing the slit raises the lower bound on the vertical momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$ under Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. The larger spread of vertical momenta makes the beam fan out more in the vertical direction after the slit.

perOption.A: Narrowing the slit increases the spread in $p_y$, causing more vertical spreading.
perOption.B: The slit confines the $y$ coordinate, so the relevant uncertainty is in $p_y$.
perOption.C: Correct. The beam spreads out more vertically.
perOption.D: The uncertainty principle applies to electrons as well as photons.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: When electrons with velocity $v$ travel through a vacuum and are incident on a thin carbon film, they produce a pattern of concentric circles on the fluorescent screen. What causes the pattern and how will the pattern change when the velocity $v$ is decreased? [Table: cause / change to pattern] A electrostatic repulsion / diameters of circles decrease. B electrostatic repulsion / diameters of circles increase. C diffraction / diameters of circles decrease. D diffraction / diameters of circles increase.

stemImage.alt: Question 28: When electrons with velocity v travel through a vacuum and are incident on a thin carbon film, they produce a pattern of concentric circles on the fluorescent s

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall of electron diffraction plus the link $\lambda = h/(mv)$.
questions.misconception: Attributing electron rings to repulsion, or getting the λ–speed trend backwards

explanation.body: The concentric rings arise from electron diffraction by the carbon film. Decreasing the electron speed reduces its momentum and increases its de Broglie wavelength, $\lambda=h/p$. The longer wavelength gives greater diffraction angles, so the rings grow in diameter.

perOption.A: This attributes the rings to electrostatic repulsion and predicts smaller rings for a longer wavelength.
perOption.B: The predicted increase in diameter is right, but electron diffraction produces the rings.
perOption.C: The longer wavelength at lower speed gives larger diffraction angles and larger rings.
perOption.D: Correct. Diffraction produces larger rings at lower speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: If the de Broglie waves associated with each of the following particles are to have the same wavelength, which particle must have the smallest velocity?
questions.stemText: If the de Broglie waves associated with each of the following particles are to have the same wavelength, which particle must have the smallest velocity? A proton B nucleus with 2 protons and 2 neutrons C electron D neutron

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: One-step use of $\lambda = h/(mv)$ comparing masses.
questions.misconception: Associating the lightest particle with the smallest velocity

explanation.body: The de Broglie relation $\lambda=h/(mv)$ gives $v=h/(m\lambda)$. At a fixed wavelength, speed is inversely proportional to mass. The helium-4 nucleus has the largest mass, so it has the smallest speed.

perOption.A: A proton is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The electron has the smallest mass and requires the greatest speed.
perOption.D: A neutron is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: When a beam of light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident normally on a plane mirror, it is reflected totally. The intensity of the light corresponds to a rate of $n$ photons per second. What is the force exerted on the mirror by the beam of light? A $nh\lambda$ B $\dfrac{nh}{\lambda}$ C $2nh\lambda$ D $\dfrac{2nh}{\lambda}$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: When a beam of light of wavelength  is incident normally on a plane mirror, it is reflected totally. The intensity of the light corresponds to a rate of n phot

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Combines photon momentum with rate of change of momentum, including the factor of 2 on reflection.
questions.misconception: Forgetting the factor of 2 for reflection, or using $p = h\lambda$

explanation.body: Each photon has momentum of magnitude $p=h/\lambda$. Total reflection reverses that momentum, so the change in momentum has magnitude $p-(-p)=2h/\lambda$. At $n$ photons per second, the force on the mirror is the rate of momentum transfer, $2nh/\lambda$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by $\lambda$ instead of dividing and omits the factor of two from reflection.
perOption.B: Counts only the incident momentum, as for absorption.
perOption.C: Accounts for the reversal but multiplies by wavelength instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: When light of a certain frequency and intensity is incident on europium metal, electrons are emitted (photoelectric effect). If the intensity of the light is increased and the frequency remains unchanged, which describes the changes observed? [Table: threshold frequency of europium / number of electrons emitted] A decreases / remains the same B decreases / increases C remains the same / remains the same D remains the same / increases

stemImage.alt: Question 27: When light of a certain frequency and intensity is incident on europium metal, electrons are observed to be emitted from the metal. This is known as the photoel

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Standard photoelectric fact: intensity affects photon rate only.
questions.misconception: Believing light intensity changes the threshold frequency or electron energy

explanation.body: The threshold frequency depends on the minimum energy required to release an electron from europium, which is independent of light intensity. At the same frequency, higher intensity means more photons reach the metal per unit time, so more electrons are emitted per unit time.

perOption.A: Incorrectly lowers the threshold and overlooks the increase in photon arrival rate.
perOption.B: Incorrectly lowers the threshold frequency when only intensity changes.
perOption.C: Overlooks the increase in electron emission rate as more photons arrive each second.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A student is given a gold-leaf electroscope and two light sources of wavelength 450 nm (blue) and 650 nm (red) to investigate the photoelectric effect of potassium and aluminium. She places the metal on the electroscope, neutralises it, and shines one of the lights on the metal. If the metal emits electrons, the gold leaf rises. [Diagram: gold-leaf electroscope with metal disc on top, metal under test placed on the disc, light incident on it.] Minimum energy to release electrons: potassium 2.3 eV, aluminium 4.3 eV. Which gives the correct observation? [Table: potassium red / potassium blue / aluminium red / aluminium blue] A does not rise / rise / does not rise / rise B does not rise / rise / does not rise / does not rise C rise / does not rise / rise / rise D rise / does not rise / rise / does not rise

stemImage.alt: Question 28: A student is given a gold-leaf electroscope and two light sources of wavelength 450 nm (blue light) and 650 nm (red light) to investigate the photoelectric effe

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Convert both wavelengths to photon energies and compare against two work functions in an unfamiliar electroscope setup.
questions.misconception: Thinking shorter wavelength light always causes emission regardless of work function

explanation.body: When electrons escape, the electroscope becomes positively charged and the gold leaf rises. Using $E=hc/\lambda$, a red photon has energy $1.9125\ \mathrm{eV}$, below both work functions. A blue photon has energy $2.7625\ \mathrm{eV}$, above potassium’s work function but below aluminium’s, so the leaf rises only for potassium under blue light.

perOption.A: Assumes blue photons can also overcome aluminium’s $4.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ work function.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the predictions for potassium and assumes both photon energies exceed aluminium’s work function.
perOption.D: Reverses the predictions for potassium and incorrectly treats red photons as energetic enough for aluminium.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A green laser pointer and a red laser pointer of the same power cast circular images on a white screen of the same diameter. The wavelengths of the green and red lasers are $\lambda_G$ and $\lambda_R$ respectively. [Diagram: two equal-sized circular spots labelled green and red.] If the pressure exerted by the green laser on the screen is $p$, what is the pressure exerted by the red laser? A $p$ B $\frac{\lambda_G}{\lambda_R}p$ C $\frac{\lambda_R}{\lambda_G}p$ D $\left(\frac{\lambda_G}{\lambda_R}\right)^2 p$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A green laser pointer and a red laser pointer of the same power cast circular images on a white screen of the same diameter. The wavelengths of the green and re

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs realising photon momentum and photon rate both depend on wavelength and cancel.
questions.misconception: Thinking pressure depends on photon momentum alone, not the photon rate

explanation.body: Each photon has momentum $h/\lambda$ and energy $hc/\lambda$, so a beam of power $P$ delivers $P/(hc/\lambda)$ photons per second. Assuming complete reflection, each photon’s momentum reverses, giving a force of $2P/c$ on the photons and an equal force magnitude on the screen. Dividing by the spot area $\pi D^2/4$ gives $8P/(c\pi D^2)$. The two beams have equal power and spot diameter, so the red beam also exerts pressure $p$.

perOption.A: Uses the momentum ratio of individual photons and overlooks the higher photon rate for red light.
perOption.B: Correct. The wavelength factors cancel.
perOption.C: Uses the photon-rate ratio and overlooks the lower momentum per red photon.
perOption.D: Squares the per-photon momentum ratio even though the force is the photon rate times the momentum change.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the 'electron cloud' in an atom?
questions.stemText: Which statement best describes the 'electron cloud' in an atom? A A shell of negative charge at a fixed radius. B A region where the electron's charge is uniformly distributed. C The path the electron follows around the nucleus. D A region where the probability of finding the electron is high.

options.label: A
options.text: A shell of negative charge at a fixed radius.

options.label: B
options.text: A region where the electron's charge is uniformly distributed.

options.label: C
options.text: The path the electron follows around the nucleus.

options.label: D
options.text: A region where the probability of finding the electron is high.

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct recall of the probabilistic interpretation of the wavefunction.
questions.misconception: Picturing the electron as following a definite orbit

explanation.body: The electron’s state is represented by a wavefunction $\psi$. Its squared magnitude $|\psi|^2$ is the probability density, and the electron cloud visualises where the electron is likely to be found.

perOption.A: Confines the electron to a single radius even though its probability density extends over a region.
perOption.B: Assumes a uniform charge distribution even though the probability density varies with position.
perOption.C: Treats the electron cloud as a classical trajectory.
perOption.D: Correct. The cloud shows where the electron is likely to be found.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron is in the $n=2$ quantum state of a one-dimensional box with kinetic energy of $6.0\ \mathrm{eV}$.

A proton is in the $n=3$ quantum state of another one-dimensional box with kinetic energy of $0.20\ \mathrm{eV}$.

What is the ratio of the width of the electron’s box to the width of the proton’s box?

A. 0.19
B. 3.5
C. 5.2
D. 7.8

stemImage.alt: Question 27: n = An electron is in the quantum state of a one-dimensional box with kinetic energy of 6.0 2 eV. n = A proton is in the quantum state of another one-dimensiona

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires rearranging the energy equation and forming a ratio involving three quantities.
questions.misconception: Omitting the quantum-number factor

explanation.body: From $E=n^2h^2/(8mL^2)$, $L=\sqrt{n^2h^2/(8mE)}\propto n/\sqrt{mE}$. Thus $L_e/L_p=(n_e/n_p)\sqrt{m_pE_p/(m_eE_e)}=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{(1.67\times10^{-27})(0.20)}{(9.11\times10^{-31})(6.0)}}=5.2113\approx5.2$.

perOption.A: Inverts the requested ratio.
perOption.B: Uses $(2/3)^2$ where the width ratio needs $2/3$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the quantum-number ratio of $2/3$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron is confined within an atom.

What is the order of magnitude of the minimum uncertainty in its momentum?

A. $10^{-48}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$
B. $10^{-24}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$
C. $10^{-20}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$
D. $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: An electron is confined within an atom. What is the order of magnitude of the minimum uncertainty in its momentum?

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires recalling the atomic length scale and using it to estimate the momentum uncertainty.
questions.misconception: Using a nuclear length scale for an atom

explanation.body: The diameter of an atom is about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, so take $\Delta x\approx10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, the minimum momentum uncertainty is of order $h/\Delta x\sim10^{-34}/10^{-10}=10^{-24}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

perOption.A: Implies a position uncertainty vastly larger than the atom.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes confinement to a much smaller distance than an atomic diameter.
perOption.D: Uses a momentum scale that would require far tighter confinement than even a nuclear diameter.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two electrons are confined along a horizontal axis. The uncertainty in the position of electron A is 0.20 nm, while the uncertainty in the position of electron B is 0.50 nm.

What is the ratio of the minimum uncertainty in the momentum of electron A to that of electron B?
questions.stemText: Two electrons are confined along a horizontal axis. The uncertainty in the position of electron A is 0.20 nm, while the uncertainty in the position of electron B is 0.50 nm. What is the ratio of the minimum uncertainty in the momentum of electron A to that of electron B? A 0.40 B 0.70 C 1.5 D 2.5

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Use the inverse relationship and keep the order of the ratio straight.
questions.misconception: Treating the two uncertainties as directly proportional

explanation.body: At the minimum momentum uncertainty, both electrons have the same position–momentum uncertainty product, so $\Delta x_A\Delta p_A=\Delta x_B\Delta p_B$. Thus $\Delta p_A/\Delta p_B=\Delta x_B/\Delta x_A=0.50/0.20=2.5$.

perOption.A: This takes the ratio of position uncertainties in the same order as the requested momentum ratio.
perOption.B: This puts the momentum ratio below one even though A has the tighter position constraint.
perOption.C: This is close to taking the square root of the inverse position ratio, but the relation is directly inverse.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and kinetic energy E?
questions.stemText: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m and kinetic energy E? A h 2 mE B 2mE h C h mE D h 2 mE

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Express momentum in terms of kinetic energy before substituting into the de Broglie equation.
questions.misconception: Inverting the de Broglie relation or dropping the kinetic energy factor of one half

explanation.body: The kinetic energy is $E=\tfrac12mv^2=(mv)^2/(2m)=p^2/(2m)$, so $p=\sqrt{2mE}$. The de Broglie relation then gives $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2mE}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This gives the inverse wavelength $p/h$.
perOption.C: This drops the factor of two when rearranging $E=p^2/(2m)$.
perOption.D: This multiplies Planck’s constant by the momentum instead of dividing by it.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The figure below shows the energy levels of the hydrogen atom.

What is the maximum number of emission spectral lines that can be observed if electrons of energy 12.9 eV are incident on the hydrogen atom in the ground state?
questions.stemText: The figure below shows the energy levels of the hydrogen atom. What is the maximum number of emission spectral lines that can be observed if electrons of energy 12.9 eV are incident on the hydrogen atom in the ground state? A 0 B 3 C 6 D 10

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires finding the highest accessible level and counting transitions between all accessible levels.
questions.misconception: Counting only transitions to the ground state

explanation.body: An incident electron can raise the atom’s energy from $-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$ to at most $-13.6+12.9=-0.7\ \mathrm{eV}$. The highest accessible level is $-0.85\ \mathrm{eV}$. The four accessible levels give six possible downward transitions, so at most six emission lines can be observed.

perOption.A: Assumes excitation requires the incident electron to give up its entire kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Counts only three transitions, for example those ending at the ground state.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Includes transitions from the inaccessible $-0.54\ \mathrm{eV}$ level.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A proton has a kinetic energy of $1.00\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of $1.0\%$, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

A $1.22\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$
B $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
C $9.08\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
D $6.59\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 29: A proton has a kinetic energy of 1.00 MeV. If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of 1.0 %, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert the energy, calculate the momentum and apply the percentage uncertainty.
questions.misconception: The full momentum can be substituted for its uncertainty.

explanation.body: Using $K=p^2/(2m)$ with $K=(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})\ \mathrm{J}$ and $m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $p=2.312\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The momentum uncertainty is $\Delta p=0.01p=2.312\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta p\,\Delta x\approx h$, the minimum position uncertainty is approximately $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Requires a much smaller momentum uncertainty than the stated 1.0% of the calculated momentum.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Is about $\sqrt{10}$ too large, consistent with a factor-of-ten underestimate of the energy in the momentum calculation.
perOption.D: Implies a momentum uncertainty larger than the full proton momentum under the syllabus estimate.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron and a proton are both accelerated from rest through the same electric potential difference.

Which row correctly compares the kinetic energy and the de Broglie wavelength of the electron and proton after the acceleration?

Option | kinetic energy | de Broglie wavelength
A | electron has greater energy | proton has longer wavelength
B | proton has greater energy | electron has longer wavelength
C | both have the same energy | proton has longer wavelength
D | both have the same energy | electron has longer wavelength

stemImage.alt: Question 28: An electron and a proton are both accelerated from rest through the same electric potential difference. Which row correctly compares the kinetic energy and the

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The comparison links energy gained through a potential difference to momentum and wavelength.
questions.misconception: Assuming equal kinetic energies imply equal momenta.

explanation.body: Both particles start from rest and gain kinetic energy $K=|q||\Delta V|$. The charge magnitudes and the magnitudes of the potential differences are equal, giving equal kinetic energies. Combining $\lambda=h/p$ with $p^2/(2m)=K$ gives $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2m|q||\Delta V|}$. The heavier proton therefore has the shorter wavelength.

perOption.A: Assigns the electron more energy and reverses the wavelength comparison.
perOption.B: Assigns the proton more energy even though both particles gain equal energy.
perOption.C: Reverses the momentum comparison at fixed kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The lighter electron has the longer wavelength.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The wave function for an electron trapped in an infinite square well is shown in the figure below.

At which position(s) is the probability of locating the electron the highest?
questions.stemText: The wave function for an electron trapped in an infinite square well is shown in the figure below. At which position(s) is the probability of locating the electron the highest? A Q only B Q and S only C P, Q and R only D P, R and T only

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recognize that the maximum and minimum of the wavefunction have the same squared magnitude.
questions.misconception: Treating the signed wavefunction as probability density.

explanation.body: Squaring the magnitude of the wavefunction gives the probability density, $|\psi|^2$. The wavefunction has its largest magnitude at Q and S, so the probability density is highest at both positions.

perOption.A: Counts the positive peak but misses the equally large magnitude at the negative trough.
perOption.B: Correct. The squared magnitude is maximal at Q and S.
perOption.C: Includes P and R, where the wavefunction is zero.
perOption.D: Selects the nodes, where the probability density is zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A proton has a kinetic energy of $1.00\ \mathrm{MeV}$. If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of $1.00\%$, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

A $4.14\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{m}$
B $1.15\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m}$
C $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
D $1.99\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 28: A proton has a kinetic energy of 1.00 MeV. If its momentum is measured with an uncertainty of 1.00 %, what is the minimum uncertainty in its position?

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Convert the proton energy to joules, calculate its momentum uncertainty, and apply the syllabus uncertainty relation.
questions.misconception: Using the full momentum or the percentage alone for momentum uncertainty.

explanation.body: From $E=p^2/(2m)$, the proton momentum is $p=\sqrt{2mE}=\sqrt{2(1.67\times10^{-27})(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})}=2.3117\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The $1.00\%$ uncertainty gives $\Delta p=2.3117\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, the minimum is about $h/\Delta p=2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses a momentum uncertainty far larger than the stated 1.00% when substituted into $h/\Delta p$.
perOption.B: Also implies a momentum uncertainty far larger than 1.00% of the calculated momentum.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the result with the syllabus uncertainty estimate.
perOption.D: Implies a smaller momentum uncertainty than the stated 1.00%.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A helium-neon laser emits red light having a wavelength of $6.4\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ and a power of $0.5\ \mathrm{mW}$.

How many photons are emitted each second?

A $1.6\times10^{15}$
B $2.6\times10^{18}$
C $1.6\times10^{21}$
D $6.4\times10^{38}$

stemImage.alt: Question 27: A helium-neon laser emits red light having a wavelength of 6.4  10−7 m and a power of 0.5 mW. How many photons are emitted each second?

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation combines photon energy from wavelength with a milliwatt-to-watt conversion.
questions.misconception: Treating power as the energy of a single photon.

explanation.body: A photon has energy $hf$, so the emission rate is $N/t=P/(hf)=P\lambda/(hc)$. Substitution gives $(0.50\times10^{-3})(6.4\times10^{-7})/[(6.63\times10^{-34})(3.0\times10^8)]=1.6\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It divides laser power by the energy per photon.
perOption.B: This rate would require about $0.81\ \mathrm{W}$ at the stated wavelength, indicating an error in the power scale.
perOption.C: Taking milli- as $10^3$ instead of $10^{-3}$ overstates the rate by a factor of $10^6$.
perOption.D: This rate implies a photon energy of about $7.8\times10^{-43}\ \mathrm{J}$, far below $hc/\lambda$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An electron, with an initial energy of $1.28\ \mathrm{eV}$, passes through a small slit of slit width $1.3\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

[The electron travels horizontally to the right towards a gap in a vertical screen. A vertical double-headed arrow marks the slit width of $1.3\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.]

What is the minimum uncertainty of the momentum of the electron as it passes through the slit?

Magnitude | Direction
A $5.1\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ | vertical
B $5.1\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ | horizontal
C $6.1\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ | vertical
D $6.1\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ | horizontal

stemImage.alt: Question 28: An electron, with an initial energy of 1.28 eV, passes through a small slit of slit width 1.3 × 10−7 m. slit width 1.3 × 10−7 m electron What is the minimum unc

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify which coordinate the slit confines before applying the uncertainty relation.
questions.misconception: Assigning the uncertainty to the direction of travel.

explanation.body: For the minimum momentum uncertainty use $\Delta x\,\Delta p\approx h$. The slit width gives $\Delta p\approx(6.63\times10^{-34})/(1.3\times10^{-7})=5.1\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The width is vertical, so the corresponding momentum uncertainty is vertical.

perOption.A: Correct. The slit width sets the vertical momentum uncertainty.
perOption.B: Uses the direction of travel for the uncertainty even though the slit confines the electron vertically.
perOption.C: Identifies the correct direction but overestimates the uncertainty given by $h/\Delta x$.
perOption.D: Overestimates $h/\Delta x$ and assigns the uncertainty to the horizontal direction.
